title: From data to a DBMS
lead: Start with a design question: what could go wrong if every feature in an application managed its own data?
goals: Distinguish a database, a DBMS, a schema, and an instance
Explain the three levels of abstraction through an example
Identify the system responsibilities behind a query

sections.title: A guide to the slides
sections.html:
A database is an organised collection of data, such as a library’s books and loans. A DBMS (Database Management System) is the software that manages how that data is stored, read, and updated. This lecture introduces the reasons for using a DBMS, the weaknesses of separate files, the view/logical/physical levels, and data independence: the ability to change one level while limiting the effect on the level above. The remaining slides cover the course roadmap, assessment, and course policies.

Read PDF pages 10–19 first; pages 21–35 provide context for the Spring 2026 course. Administrative dates belong to that historical slide edition and are not current submission deadlines.

Data model, schema and instance

A data model supplies concepts for representing data: relational attributes and tuples, graph vertices and edges, or document fields. A schema chooses a particular structure within that model. Book(book_id, title) and Loan(book_id, member_id) are a library schema; their current rows are an instance. A shop can use Product and Order in the same relational model with a different schema.

A DBMS centralizes constraints, concurrent updates and atomic multi-step changes. An index can locate a key without a complete file scan, and a query interface can answer new questions without a separate file-processing program for each one. Access controls can distinguish public catalogue data from borrower records. These are mechanisms that must be configured correctly; choosing a database does not automatically secure an application.

Check: do a library and a shop need different data models?

Worked answer. They can both use the relational model while selecting different schemas and storing different instances.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19 ↗. The worked examples are original.

sections.title: Original design exercise: a neighbourhood library
sections.html:
An original scenario. A library keeps books.csv and loans.csv. Initially, a book has identifier B17 and its loan also refers to B17. Mai changes the identifier in the books file to B017, but the program stops before updating the loans file: the loan still refers to B17, an identifier that no longer exists. Someone else then overwrites loans.csv with an older copy, making a new loan disappear.

  1. Draw the data before and after each write. Identify exactly which relationship is lost.
  2. Write the business rules: every loan must refer to an existing book; assuming each book identifier represents one physical copy, each copy may have only one open loan.
  3. Distinguish a modelling error, an update-procedure error, and an error caused by two people writing concurrently.

Analysis. The rule that a book identifier must exist is a data constraint. Changing a book identifier and updating its related loans should form one transaction, a unit of work containing several operations: either both changes finish, or no partial update remains. Overwriting the current file with an older copy is an access-coordination problem. Later lectures introduce the specific transaction mechanisms.

Key takeaway

Changing the file format does not fix update errors. Both CSV and JSON can contain broken references or suffer overwritten changes. The system needs constraint checking, all-or-nothing updates, and coordinated writes.

sections.title: Three views of the same system
sections.html:
An original example. A librarian sees borrowers’ names and due dates; visitors searching the catalogue see only book titles and availability. This is the view level: each user group sees the data relevant to it. At the logical level, we describe Book(book_id, title) and Loan(book_id, borrower, due). At the physical level, we decide how records and indexes, the structures that help locate data, are arranged.

Book(book_id, title) is a schema: it describes the table’s columns and structure. The current rows, such as (B017, “Databases”), form an instance: the data at a particular moment. Adding a book changes the instance; adding a publication-year column changes the schema.

Key takeaway

A schema describes structure; an instance is the current data. Distinguishing these changes helps you decide whether an application needs another data row or a new structure for representing its data.

Ask yourself: should changing the page size, the unit managed during reads and writes, from 4 KiB to 8 KiB force the catalogue application to rewrite its queries? Physical data independence helps keep logical queries stable when storage details change.

Check yourself: at which level do we add a borrower’s email address?

Adding the email field changes the logical description of the data. Its storage offset is a physical detail. Deciding who may see it belongs to view and access-control design.

sections.title: A roadmap for independent practice
sections.html:
The exercises on this website use new examples and are not official assessed submissions: ask a data question → write a relational expression → count page I/Os → design buffers and indexes → choose an execution plan → preserve correct results under concurrency and failures.

Before Lecture 2, write a plain-language question about the library and state its expected answer for three data rows. You do not need an algorithm yet. That expected answer will help you check the execution methods introduced later.

Follow a request through the DBMS layers

Query planning parses a query, checks its meaning and selects a physical plan. Operator execution performs scans, filters and joins. File and index management locates logical records; buffer management manages frames and replacement; disk-space management maps page IDs to storage and performs reads or writes. These are responsibilities and interfaces, not necessarily five separate operating-system processes. Concurrency and recovery coordinate work across layers.

For an index lookup whose data page is absent from RAM, file/index management requests a buffer frame, buffer management obtains the page through disk-space management, and execution examines the record. A cache hit avoids that data-page read. Planning chooses the access path; the buffer manager does not choose whether an index is semantically appropriate.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 ↗. The worked examples are original.

Workload and storage architecture are separate choices

OLTP usually means many short transactions that touch small amounts of data. OLAP usually means broad analytical queries; HTAP combines transactional and analytical work. Those describe workloads. Disk-oriented and in-memory describe storage architecture. A disk-oriented DBMS can cache a working set in RAM even when its database is much larger than RAM. An in-memory working set still needs a persistence strategy for durability.

Row layouts tend to serve operations on a whole entity; column layouts tend to serve scans of a few attributes across many entities. These are workload tendencies, not rules forbidding transactions on columns or analysis on rows. If every needed page is already cached, this particular execution may avoid disk reads while the DBMS remains disk-oriented. Ordinary RAM is volatile; a successful write to RAM alone is not a durable commit.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 11, 12, 13, 14 ↗ · Physical PDF pp. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 11, 12, 16 ↗. The worked examples are original.

quiz.question: Changing a record’s byte position primarily belongs to which level?
quiz.explanation: A byte position is a physical representation detail; the schema describes the meaning and structure of the data.
